figures.alt: The Greenhouse effect, IGCSE & GCSE Biology revision notes

specPoints.text: know that carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and that increasing amounts in the atmosphere may contribute to climate change

primer.text: From Composition of Air you already know that carbon dioxide sits in air only as a small share, yet you have also seen it named as a greenhouse gas with a large warming role. This note explains how greenhouse gases keep the Earth warm enough for life, where atmospheric carbon dioxide comes from, and why rising amounts matter for the climate.

lessons.title: What is the greenhouse effect?
lessons.opening: Greenhouse gases maintain temperatures on Earth high enough to support life, and this warming is known as the greenhouse effect. Three greenhouse gases of record are carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. The mechanism is a two-step exchange: short wavelength radiation arrives from the sun, and the warmed surface re-emits it as long wavelength radiation that greenhouse gases trap and store.
keyPoints: Greenhouse gases keep temperatures on Earth high enough to support life.
This natural warming of the planet is known as the greenhouse effect.
Three greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour.
Short wavelength radiation from the sun strikes the surface and some is re-emitted as long wavelength radiation.
Greenhouse gases trap much of that re-emitted energy, absorbing and storing it in the atmosphere.

low.restatement: Some gases in the air let sunshine in but hold the warmth in, like a blanket around the planet. That trapped warmth is the greenhouse effect, and it keeps the Earth warm enough to live on.
low.analogy: A car parked in the sun with its windows up gets warmer inside than out; the glass lets light in and slows the heat leaving, just as greenhouse gases do for the Earth.
low.examPointer: Name carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour when asked for greenhouse gases, and describe the warming as the greenhouse effect.

medium.restatement: The sun emits short wavelength radiation, part of which the surface absorbs and re-emits as long wavelength radiation. Greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, absorb and store much of that outgoing energy, and the resulting trapped heat keeps global temperatures in the range that supports life.
medium.analogy: Picture a one-way turnstile at a stadium exit: crowds stream in freely but file out slowly, so the arena stays full of warmth, exactly as the atmosphere holds its heat.
medium.examPointer: Full answers pair the two wavelength names with what happens to each: short wavelength arrives from the sun, long wavelength leaves the surface and is trapped.

check.stem: Why is the greenhouse effect essential for life on Earth?

options.text: Because it maintains temperatures high enough to support life
options.explanation: Without the trapped warmth the planet would be far too cold, so the effect is a life-supporting feature, not a flaw.

options.text: Because it blocks all sunlight from reaching the ground
options.explanation: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere; the effect concerns the heat leaving, not the light arriving.

options.text: Because it produces the oxygen animals breathe
options.explanation: Oxygen comes from photosynthesis; the greenhouse effect is about temperature, not gas supply.

options.text: Because it removes carbon dioxide from the air
options.explanation: Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide; they trap heat rather than remove it from the air.

check.stem: Which set names three greenhouse gases?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour
options.explanation: These three are the greenhouse gases named in the note, each able to absorb and store outgoing energy.

options.text: Nitrogen, oxygen and argon
options.explanation: Those are the main components of air, but they are not the heat-trapping gases named here.
options.misconception: abundant gases confused with greenhouse gases

options.text: Chlorine, bromine and iodine
options.explanation: The halogens are reactive non-metals from another topic and are not atmospheric greenhouse gases.

options.text: Hydrogen, helium and neon
options.explanation: None of these is named as a greenhouse gas; hydrogen is barely present in air and the others are noble gases.

check.stem: What happens to short wavelength radiation from the sun when it strikes the Earth's surface?

options.text: Some is absorbed and some is re-emitted as long wavelength radiation
options.explanation: The surface takes in part of the incoming energy and sends energy back out at a longer wavelength.

options.text: All of it reflects straight back into space unchanged
options.explanation: If everything reflected, the surface would not warm; the absorption and re-emission steps are what drive the effect.
options.misconception: surface treated as a perfect mirror

options.text: It turns into oxygen through the reaction
options.explanation: No gas is made from light at the surface; the energy simply changes wavelength on re-emission.

options.text: It is stored forever inside the ground
options.explanation: The surface re-emits the energy; the trapping happens in the atmosphere, not underground.

check.stem: What do greenhouse gases do to the long wavelength radiation leaving the surface?

options.text: They absorb and store much of it, trapping the energy inside the atmosphere
options.explanation: This absorption and storage is exactly what keeps the trapped warmth in place around the planet.

options.text: They speed it up so it escapes faster into space
options.explanation: The opposite happens; the gases slow the energy's departure by absorbing and storing it.

options.text: They change it into visible light
options.explanation: No wavelength conversion is claimed; the gases absorb and store the energy as it is.

options.text: They have no effect on it at all
options.explanation: If they had no effect there would be no greenhouse effect and no trapped warmth.

check.stem: A student says the greenhouse effect is entirely harmful. What is the correct verdict?

options.text: Wrong: the natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life, though rising gas amounts may contribute to climate change
options.explanation: The effect itself is life-supporting; the concern is the enhanced effect from increasing gas levels, not the natural warming.

options.text: Correct: any trapped heat damages the planet
options.explanation: The natural level of trapped heat is essential; harm comes from extra trapping above that level.

options.text: Correct, because greenhouse gases destroy the ozone layer
options.explanation: Ozone depletion is a separate atmospheric problem; the greenhouse effect concerns trapped heat, not ozone.

options.text: The claim cannot be judged from chemistry alone
options.explanation: The note settles it directly: the effect maintains life-supporting temperatures, so it is not simply harmful.

lessons.title: Carbon dioxide
lessons.opening: Carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere from several directions: the combustion of wood and fossil fuels, the respiration of plants and animals, and the thermal decomposition of carbonate rocks together with the effect of acids on carbonates. Although it is present in only small amounts, increasing levels of carbon dioxide and methane are upsetting natural conditions by trapping extra heat energy, and increasing amounts may contribute to climate change.
keyPoints: Combustion of wood and fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
Respiration of plants and animals is another source of atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Carbonate rocks breaking down with heat, and acids acting on carbonates, also free the gas.
Carbon dioxide and methane are present in only small amounts yet trap extra heat energy.
Rising carbon dioxide levels in the air may help drive climate change.

low.restatement: Burning fuels and wood, living things respiring, and carbonates breaking down or meeting acids all put carbon dioxide into the air. More of the gas traps more heat, which may push the climate to change.
low.analogy: Like adding one more blanket each winter: each addition is small, but the house keeps getting warmer with every layer.
low.examPointer: Learn the three source families and link them to the rising amount; questions often ask for sources and consequence in one answer.

medium.restatement: The atmosphere gains carbon dioxide from combustion of wood and fossil fuels, from respiration of plants and animals, and from carbonate rocks breaking down with heat or meeting acids. Because the gas absorbs and stores outgoing energy even at low concentrations, its rising level, with methane's, traps extra heat and may contribute to climate change.
medium.analogy: Think of a small leak with a big flood: the gas is a tiny share of the air, yet the extra warmth it traps grows with every added portion.
medium.examPointer: Quote sources and effect together, and remember the wording is may contribute, which matches the measured caution of the specification.

check.stem: Which source adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere through burning?

options.text: Combustion of wood and fossil fuels
options.explanation: Burning wood and fossil fuels joins their carbon to oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide.

options.text: Evaporation of sea water
options.explanation: Evaporation moves water vapour into the air; it carries no carbon into the atmosphere.
options.misconception: water cycle confused with carbon sources

options.text: Lightning fixing nitrogen
options.explanation: Lightning oxides nitrogen, which concerns nitrogen compounds, not carbon dioxide.

options.text: Photosynthesis in green plants
options.explanation: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air; it is the counter-process, not a source.

check.stem: How do living things contribute atmospheric carbon dioxide?

options.text: Through the respiration of plants and animals
options.explanation: Respiration releases carbon dioxide, so every breathing organism feeds this source.

options.text: Through the digestion of rocks by burrowing animals
options.explanation: No such route exists; the living-world contribution named is respiration.

options.text: Through decay releasing pure carbon powder
options.explanation: The named contribution is respiration; carbon powder is not what living things release.

options.text: Living things contribute nothing to atmospheric carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Respiration by plants and animals is one of the three source families named.

check.stem: Why can a small amount of atmospheric carbon dioxide still have a large warming effect?

options.text: Because it absorbs and stores the outgoing long wavelength energy very effectively
options.explanation: Effectiveness per molecule matters more than abundance; a small share of an efficient absorber traps much heat.

options.text: Because its molecules are the largest in the atmosphere
options.explanation: Molecule size is not the mechanism; the ability to absorb and store outgoing energy is.

options.text: Because it is heavier than nitrogen and sinks onto cities
options.explanation: Gases mix through the atmosphere; the warming is global trapping, not local pooling.

options.text: Because it burns when ignited
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide does not burn; it is already the fully burnt oxide of carbon.

check.stem: Which pairing of carbonate reactions both release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere?

options.text: Thermal decomposition of carbonate rocks and the effect of acids on carbonates
options.explanation: Both routes break carbonates and free their carbon as carbon dioxide.

options.text: Freezing of carbonate rocks and their erosion by wind
options.explanation: Neither freezing nor wind erosion is named as a carbon dioxide source; heat and acids are.
options.misconception: weathering confused with the named routes

options.text: Burning of carbonate rocks and their dissolving in sea water
options.explanation: The named routes are thermal decomposition and acid attack, not burning or sea-water dissolving.

options.text: Carbonate rocks release no carbon dioxide at all
options.explanation: Both named routes show that carbonates do release the gas into the atmosphere.

check.stem: What consequence does the specification attach to increasing amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide?

options.text: They may contribute to climate change
options.explanation: The of-record wording says the rising level may contribute to climate change, matching the extra trapped heat.

options.text: They will thicken the ozone layer
options.explanation: Ozone is a separate issue; carbon dioxide's named consequence concerns climate.

options.text: They will make the air toxic to breathe
options.explanation: The air stays breathable; the concern is trapped heat and climate, not direct toxicity at these levels.

options.text: They have no consequence because the share is tiny
options.explanation: The small share does not prevent a warming consequence; the specification names climate change.
options.misconception: share size used to dismiss effect

glossary.definition: A gas that absorbs and stores outgoing energy from the Earth's surface, keeping the planet warm.
Energy travelling as waves; short wavelength radiation arrives from the sun and long wavelength radiation leaves the surface.
A greenhouse gas, present in small amounts, whose rising level adds to the trapped heat.
The process by which living things release energy, giving out carbon dioxide as they do so.
The long-term shift in the Earth's climate that increasing greenhouse gas levels may contribute to.

workedExample.prompt: a) Name three greenhouse gases. b) Describe how greenhouse gases keep the Earth warm, using the terms short wavelength and long wavelength radiation. c) Give one source of atmospheric carbon dioxide and state the possible consequence of its rising concentration.
steps: a) Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are greenhouse gases.
b) Short wavelength radiation from the Sun passes into the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface; the surface re-emits the energy as long wavelength radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb and store much of that outgoing long wavelength radiation, trapping the heat — the greenhouse effect keeps temperatures high enough to support life.
c) Combustion of wood and fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere; increasing amounts trap extra heat energy and may contribute to climate change.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) CO2, methane and water vapour. b) They absorb and store the long wavelength radiation re-emitted by the warmed surface. c) Fossil-fuel combustion; rising CO2 may contribute to climate change.
